key_concept: For separated lenses, apply the lens formula $\frac{1}{v}-\frac{1}{u}=\frac{1}{f}$ to each lens in turn; the image formed by the first lens is the object for the second.
steps: Use the Cartesian sign convention with light travelling left to right. The two lenses are 3 cm apart, so they are not in contact and must be treated one at a time.
Lens $L_1$: $u_1=-30$ cm and $f_1=+10$ cm. Then $\frac{1}{v_1}=\frac{1}{f_1}+\frac{1}{u_1}=\frac{1}{10}-\frac{1}{30}=\frac{2}{30}$, so $v_1=+15$ cm, i.e. 15 cm to the right of $L_1$.
$L_2$ is only 3 cm to the right of $L_1$. The rays are intercepted before they converge, so the image $I_1$ acts as a virtual object for $L_2$.
This virtual object lies $15-3=12$ cm to the right of $L_2$, so $u_2=+12$ cm.
The negative sign means the final image is 60 cm to the left of the concave lens, and it is virtual.
final_answer: Option (2): 60 cm to the left of the concave lens
why_not_others: Option (4) comes from taking $u_2=-12$ (treating the virtual object as real) or dropping the sign of $v_2$. Option (3) comes from wrongly using the contact formula ($P=0$) or mishandling the 3 cm gap.
common_trap: Students often use $\frac{1}{F}=\frac{1}{f_1}+\frac{1}{f_2}$, which gives zero power, or forget that the intermediate image beyond $L_2$ is a virtual object with positive $u$.
time_saving_tip: Find $v_1$ quickly (object at $3f$ gives the image at $1.5f=15$ cm). Then $u_2=+12$, and $\frac{1}{12}-\frac{1}{10}=-\frac{1}{60}$ gives the answer at once.
